title: Tulane studies, Two Bits clubs and the 1932 Rose Bowl trip
summary: Hirsch left Tulane architecture to play music, played Two Bits clubs and Honeysuckle Inn, had a drum shop and timpani, and went to the Rose Bowl with the Tulane band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I lived, I lived too far uptown for it. I didn't live in that, live in that section. Where were you living then? On Napoleon Avenue. On Jefferson Avenue. In the uptown Tulane section, the university section. But, uh. You went to Tulane, didn't you? Mm-hmm. Two years, until I found out that if I graduated I could get a job as a, as a brassman for fifteen dollars a week. So I said, I'm making sixty dollars a week playing music. I think I'm gonna stay with the music. No, I was, it was, this was just about in time for the, 19, I would have graduated in thirty. Which, uh. I didn't feel like waiting that long to go broke. Because thirty was a bad year in New Orleans. And I did, I was doing, I always did fairly well as far as music was concerned. In fact, in those days I was playing out at the, uh, we getting into another era of the, of the, uh, back here on the, uh, Two Bits Clubs. Uh-huh. Honeysuckle Inn. That was another era. The Two Bits Clubs, Honeysuckle Inn, there was an Owls Orchestra played over there for a while. They played at the Honeysuckle Inn. That was about a six piece band. Who else played there? Where? Uh, Louis Primal. Louis Primal? Louis Primal used to play there. Frank Federico used to play with Louis. I was across the street at the, Two Bits Club. I can't remember the name of it. In fact, that, that's when I was gonna quit to go and sell shoes for $15 a week. From the eight in the morning till five in the afternoon. And I decided not to. I was making $65 a week then. I was, I was a piano player and I was, I had to accompany Al Moore, who was a trombone player, used to sing between sets. He'd go around with his trombone and sing. And he'd split tips with me. So I made, I was making around $35, $40 a week in tips and $35 a week playing piano. So I said, I think I'll stay with this.
Did you study music at all at Tulane while you were there?

No, I was in architecture. Uh huh. I was in, in architecture. In fact, the, the timpanis that they got at Tulane were bought from me. Were bought from you? For me. For you. For me. I had a set of, first set of pedal timpanis in New Orleans. And, uh, and, uh, picked them out and they ordered them and bought them. And, uh, I was, uh, well I played with the Tulane band. Who was the band director at that time? Dr. Martin Tenhor. And then, uh, after that was, uh, Dr. When we went to California. I went to, I went to the Rose Bowl with him. In 32. Well I was, I was, uh, in charge of the drum section. In fact, uh, in those days we had, uh, and I had a, I had a drum shop in New Orleans. I had a drum shop. I used to repair drums and heads. Of course, in those days, you go out in the rain with a snare drum or a bass drum. You come in the next day and have a new head put in it. That was calfskin heads. Today it's no longer like that. Today you got, uh, today you got plastic heads. You can go in a rainstorm, you can put it in a tub. A tub of water and it won't hurt the, won't hurt the, uh, won't hurt the, uh, skins. But, uh, I went, when I was at the Sang of Theater in 1932 when we went to the Rose Bowl. I took off for two weeks and went with the Tulane band to, uh, to the Rose Bowl. It was a fantastic trip.
